author: Declaration Desk
title: Adhikari tells Cooch Behar police to trace and send back Muslim migrants from Bangladesh
dek: At the Rash Mela, the chief minister said Hindus who crossed the border were refugees to be sheltered, and asked police and the BSF to work together on the frontier. The opposition had not responded by Thursday morning.
body:
West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Wednesday directed police in Cooch Behar to identify Muslims who, he said, had entered the district illegally from Bangladesh and to send them back by the routes they came in, while describing Hindus who had crossed the border as refugees who must be sheltered.

"Illegal Muslim infiltrators from Bangladesh have to be identified and traced, one by one, in this district," Mr Adhikari, who also holds the home portfolio, said at a programme in Cooch Behar during his visit for the town's Rash Mela, according to reports. "Those Hindus who have come from across the border are not infiltrators. They are refugees," he said.

## What he said

Mr Adhikari addressed his instructions to the Cooch Behar superintendent of police, Manish Joshi, according to reports. He asked the state police and the Border Security Force (BSF) to coordinate closely on the international border, and said the state had handed over land to the BSF for fencing and border infrastructure, so that smuggling should stop once the fencing was complete. Reports did not give the area of land transferred.

He also asked police to act against what he called illegal madrasas in border areas, and against cannabis cultivation, fake currency and drug trafficking.

At the same visit, Mr Adhikari blamed the CPI(M), which ruled Bengal from 1977 to 2011, for the loss of land by Rajbanshi and tribal families. "In the name of land reform through the Barga Act, the CPI(M) took away the land" of tribal families, he said, according to reports, and said his government would examine Rajbanshi demands, including adding the Rajbanshi language to the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. The CPI(M) has rejected the claim that Left-era land reforms transferred Rajbanshi land to Bangladeshi migrants and asked for documentary proof, according to reports.

The Trinamool Congress, the main opposition party in the Assembly, had not publicly responded to the remarks by Thursday morning. Reports describe only directions from the chief minister; no arrests or deportations under them had been reported.

## The legal position

Cooch Behar shares a long land border with Bangladesh, much of it in riverine and enclave areas that are hard to fence. Under Indian law, a person suspected of being a foreign national must prove their citizenship, but courts have repeatedly held that due process must be followed before anyone is deported.

The Calcutta High Court has already intervened in at least one Cooch Behar case. Earlier this month, a vacation bench barred the authorities from pushing a woman and her two children, who held Indian passports, across the border into Bangladesh, ruling that people holding Indian passports cannot be deported as suspected foreigners without first being given a chance to prove their citizenship.

## Why it matters

The remarks come at a delicate moment for relations with Dhaka. The two governments have yet to begin talks on the Ganges water-sharing treaty, which expires on 12 December, and the question of people being sent across the border has been a recurring irritant between them. Bangladesh had not commented on Mr Adhikari's remarks by Thursday morning.

The distinction he drew between Muslim and Hindu migrants mirrors the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, which offers a fast track to citizenship to Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan who entered India before 31 December 2014. Critics of the law have argued that excluding Muslims is discriminatory; the central government has said the law protects persecuted minorities and takes away no one's citizenship. Challenges to the Act are pending in the Supreme Court.
